events.title: Earliest Settlers
events.description: Archaeological evidence indicates that Micronesian and Polynesian peoples arrived on Nauru around 1000 BCE, becoming the island's first inhabitants. These early settlers likely came from the Solomon Islands and Bismarck Archipelago, crossing the Pacific in outrigger canoes. They brought agricultural techniques, fishing skills, and unique cultural traditions. Though Nauru spans only 21 square kilometers, its rich marine resources and favorable climate attracted these seafaring peoples. Early inhabitants developed a lifestyle adapted to the small island environment, establishing the foundation for a civilization lasting thousands of years.

events.title: Formation of Unique Culture
events.description: Nauruans gradually developed a unique language, social structure, and cultural traditions. The Nauruan language belongs to the Austronesian Micronesian branch, connected to but distinct from other Micronesian languages. Islanders developed a matrilineal social structure where land and property passed through the mother's line. They created unique music, dance, and oral legends recording ethnic history and mythology. Nauruans practiced animism, worshiping ancestors and natural spirits. The cultural traditions formed during this period became core to Nauruan ethnic identity, with lasting influence to this day.

events.title: Establishment of Twelve Tribe System
events.description: Nauruan society gradually evolved into a confederation of twelve independent tribes (Eamwit, Eamwidamit, Eamwit, Eano, Emangum, Emeo, Eoraru, Iruwa, Irutsi, Iwi, Ranibok, Deiboe). Each tribe controlled specific island territory with its own leader and clan totem. Tribes maintained connections through complex kinship relations, intermarriage, and ritual exchanges. This tribal system provided framework for social organization and land management, ensuring equitable resource distribution. Tribal elder councils handled major island matters, forming a parliament-like decision-making mechanism. The twelve-tribe system became the foundation of traditional Nauruan society until gradual dissolution during the European colonial period.

events.title: Development of Fishing Techniques
events.description: Nauruans developed sophisticated fishing techniques, including the unique method of using trained frigate birds to assist fishing. They domesticated frigate birds, utilizing the birds' ability to locate fish schools. When birds found schools they returned to boats, allowing fishermen to follow. Nauruans also crafted refined hooks, nets and fish traps, using outrigger canoes for lagoon and offshore fishing. They mastered lunar phases, tides and seasonal effects on fish behavior, developing rich ocean knowledge. These fishing techniques not only provided food but became important components of Nauruan culture, with related knowledge passed through oral tradition across generations.

events.title: Agriculture and Sustainable Living
events.description: Nauruans developed sustainable agricultural systems adapted to the small island environment. They cultivated coconut palms, pandanus, bananas and taro. Coconuts provided food, drink, building materials and rope fibers. Pandanus fruit and leaves were widely utilized, with leaves woven into mats, baskets and roof coverings. Nauruans grew taro and other root crops in fertile land around Buada Lagoon. They practiced crop rotation and fallowing to protect soil fertility. Limited land resources prompted Nauruans to develop refined land management and resource conservation traditions, ensuring small island ecosystem balance and long-term tribal survival.

events.title: Intertribal Conflict and Peace
events.description: Though the twelve tribes usually maintained peaceful coexistence, conflicts occasionally arose over land, resources or honor. Intertribal disputes were primarily resolved through negotiation and mediation, but sometimes escalated to armed conflict. Nauruans used spears, clubs and slingshots as weapons. However, the island's limited space and interdependent relationships constrained large-scale warfare. Tribes developed complex diplomatic etiquette and mediation mechanisms, including formal apology ceremonies, compensation systems and peace treaties. These traditions promoted social stability, maintaining long-term peace. Intertribal competition also manifested peacefully, such as singing contests, dance performances and athletic competitions.

events.title: First European Contact
events.description: Captain John Fearn of the British whaling ship HMS Hunter became the first European recorded as having discovered Nauru. Passing Nauru on his voyage to Guangzhou, China, he was drawn by the island's lush vegetation and friendly inhabitants and named it "Pleasant Island." Captain Fearn's record marked Nauru's entry into the view of the Western world. However, because of Nauru's remote location and lack of natural harbors, few European ships visited in the first few decades. The name "Pleasant Island" was adopted on European navigation charts, and Nauru's traditional name remained unknown in the West for a long time. This contact opened a new chapter in Nauru's history, although its effects were not obvious in the first decades.

events.title: Era of Whalers and Traders
events.description: In the mid-19th century, whaling ships, traders and drifters began visiting Nauru more frequently. Europeans and Americans came for fresh water, food and timber supplies. They exchanged tobacco, alcohol, firearms and metal tools with Nauruans. These foreign items quickly transformed Nauruan society. Firearms introduction disrupted traditional power balance; alcohol caused social problems. Foreign diseases like influenza, measles and venereal diseases spread among islanders without immunity, causing population decline. Some European deserters and traders permanently settled in Nauru, intermarrying with local women and becoming cultural intermediaries. This period saw Nauru begin integrating into the global economic system, but at the cost of traditional lifestyle destruction and catastrophic population decline.

events.title: Ten Years Tribal War
events.description: Firearms introduction plunged Nauru into a devastating ten-year civil war, known as the 'Ten Years War' or 'Tribal War.' Traditional conflict resolution mechanisms collapsed before modern weapons. The twelve tribes split into two major alliances, engaging in bloody combat. War caused about 500 deaths, over one-third of the population. Many traditional leaders were killed, social structure verged on collapse. During war, islanders purchased more firearms and ammunition from foreign merchants, intensifying conflict. Agricultural and fishing production disrupted, islanders' lives fell into hardship. Exhausted tribal leaders eventually requested German intervention to end chaos. This catastrophic war became a turning point in Nauruan history, paving the way for German colonial rule and fundamentally changing the island's fate.

events.title: German Annexation of Nauru
events.description: At the request of Nauruan chiefs to end tribal wars, the German Empire formally declared Nauru its protectorate, incorporating it into German New Guinea. Germany dispatched colonial officials and a police force, confiscated all firearms, and restored order. The Germans established a colonial administration and appointed district officers to run the island. They introduced the German legal system but retained some traditional chiefly powers as instruments of indirect rule. German missionaries arrived and began the process of Christianization. The German colonial government built schools, hospitals, and infrastructure on the island. Colonial rule ended Nauruan self-rule but also brought peace and stability. The Germans began to survey the island's natural resources, and these surveys eventually led to the discovery of phosphate deposits, which completely changed Nauru's fate.

events.title: Spread of Christianity
events.description: German Protestant missionaries and Catholic priests established mission stations in Nauru, beginning systematic spread of Christianity. They learned Nauruan language, translated the Bible into local language, and built churches and schools. Christian doctrine conflicted and fused with Nauruan traditional beliefs. Many Nauruans converted to Christianity but also retained some traditional beliefs and customs, forming unique religious syncretism. Church schools taught German, arithmetic and Western knowledge, cultivating new generation of Western-educated Nauruan elite. Christianity's spread changed Nauru's social structure, moral norms and cultural practices. Churches became important social institutions, playing key roles in Nauru's modernization. By early 20th century, most Nauruans were at least nominally Christian.

events.title: Discovery of Phosphate Deposits
events.description: Albert Ellis, a New Zealand geologist working for the Pacific Phosphate Company, discovered large deposits of high-quality phosphate on Nauru. The discovery came by chance: Ellis noticed that a rock brought from Nauru to Sydney and used as a doorstop was in fact phosphate-rich rock. Chemical analysis confirmed that Nauru had one of the finest phosphate deposits in the world, with phosphate content as high as 85 percent. The phosphate had formed over millions of years from the accumulation of seabird droppings and geological processes. Phosphate is an important agricultural fertilizer, and demand surged during the global agricultural expansion of the early 20th century. The discovery completely changed the trajectory of Nauru's history, turning this remote island into a focus of global mining and imperialist competition and beginning a century-long era of extraction.

events.title: Pacific Phosphate Company Established
events.description: Britain, Australia and New Zealand jointly established Pacific Phosphate Company, obtaining German government-granted rights to mine phosphate on Nauru and neighboring Ocean Island (Banaba). Company paid Nauruan landowners extremely low royalties, only half-penny per ton, far below mineral actual value. Company began large-scale mining operations, constructing wharves, railways, processing facilities and worker camps. Hundreds of contract laborers from China, Japan and other Pacific islands were brought in, forming diverse ethnic community. Phosphate mining quickly became island's dominant industry, but profits primarily flowed to foreign companies and colonial government. Nauruans were marginalized, losing land but gaining little benefit. This marked beginning of Nauru's economic colonization, laying foundation for later environmental destruction and economic dependency.

events.title: Australian Occupation in the First World War
events.description: After the outbreak of the First World War, the Australian Naval and Military Expeditionary Force quickly occupied Nauru in September 1914 without meeting resistance. German colonial officials were expelled, ending German rule on Nauru. Australian military authorities took over the administration of the island, maintaining order and phosphate mining operations. During the war, phosphate exports continued, mainly to Australia and New Zealand, supporting agricultural production and the war effort of the Allies. The Australian occupation marked Nauru's transfer from the German sphere of influence into the British imperial system. For the Nauruans it was merely a change of colonial master, and their lives and rights were not substantially improved. After the war, Australia refused to return Nauru to Germany and instead sought permanent control of this lucrative phosphate island.

events.title: British Phosphate Commissioners Established
events.description: Australian, British and New Zealand governments jointly formed British Phosphate Commissioners (BPC), taking over Pacific Phosphate Company assets and mining rights. This joint government agency monopolized phosphate mining on Nauru and Ocean Island, aimed at ensuring British Empire nations obtained fertilizer supplies at preferential prices. BPC possessed greater power than private companies, exercising stricter control over Nauru. Commission dramatically expanded mining scale, building more infrastructure, bringing in more foreign workers. Nauruan landowners' royalties remained extremely low, far insufficient to compensate land loss and environmental destruction. BPC establishment marked Nauru's complete integration into British imperial economic system, becoming mineral colony serving metropole interests. This exploitative system persisted for decades, causing profound economic and social consequences.

events.title: League of Nations Mandate
events.description: After the Treaty of Versailles, the League of Nations designated Nauru a "Class C mandate," administered by Britain on behalf of Australia, Britain, and New Zealand jointly, with actual administration carried out by Australia. This arrangement gave Australia legal control over Nauru while avoiding the international criticism of outright annexation. The terms of the mandate required the administering power to promote the welfare of the islanders, but these obligations were often ignored. Australia set up a full colonial administration on Nauru, with an Administrator as the supreme authority. Traditional chiefs were reduced to an advisory role, and real power lay in the hands of colonial officials. The mandate system was nominally for the "civilizing mission" and preparing for self-government, but in practice it was a disguise for imperialist control. The Nauruans took no part in deciding their own fate and became pawns in international political bargaining.

events.title: Nauru Local Government Council Established
events.description: Australian colonial authorities established Nauru Local Government Council, composed of elected Nauruan representatives, serving as advisory body. This was first time Nauruans obtained some form of political representation, but power was extremely limited, only able to advise colonial Administrator on local matters, without legislative or executive power. Council mainly handled community affairs, traditional customs and small-scale public works. Major decisions, especially regarding phosphate mining and economic policy, remained completely controlled by colonial authorities. Nevertheless, local council became training ground for Nauruan political elite, cultivating leaders who later led independence movement. Council establishment reflected colonizers' desire to create facade of political participation while maintaining absolute control. It was Nauru's first step toward self-government, though the road remained long.

events.title: Population Nadir and Health Crisis
events.description: Due to introduced diseases in late 19th and early 20th centuries, population losses from tribal warfare, and low birth rates, Nauru's indigenous population hit historic low in 1932, only about 1,500 people. Compared to pre-contact estimated population of 3,000-4,000, this meant Nauruan nation faced survival crisis. Foreign diseases especially tuberculosis, influenza and dysentery continued plaguing community. Colonial government's medical services were insufficient, mainly serving white administrators and foreign miners. High infant mortality and low fertility rates threatened Nauruan nation's future. This population crisis drew attention from Nauruan leaders and some humanitarians. Colonial government was eventually forced to improve medical services and public health. From late 1930s, with better healthcare and improved living conditions, population began slowly recovering. This dark period left deep trauma, affecting Nauru's demographic structure and social psychology.

events.title: German Raiders' Bombardment
events.description: During the Second World War, the German auxiliary cruisers Komet and Orion in turn shelled Nauru, destroying phosphate facilities, oil storage tanks, and harbor installations. The raids aimed to disrupt the Allied phosphate supply. Five ships at anchor were sunk, shore facilities were badly damaged, and several people were killed. Phosphate exports were interrupted for months. The raids exposed Nauru's vulnerability as a strategic resource island. The Australian government recognized the need to strengthen its defenses, but resources were limited and the focus was on other theaters. The raids caused panic on Nauru, and the islanders for the first time directly experienced the horrors of modern war. After the facilities were repaired, phosphate production resumed, but the shadow of war hung over the island. This incident foreshadowed a far more serious disaster to come: the Japanese invasion and occupation. The German raids were the prelude to Nauru's experience of the Second World War.

events.title: Japanese Occupation of Nauru
events.description: Japanese Imperial Navy marines landed on Nauru; the Australian garrison was too small to resist, and the island was quickly occupied. The Japanese took over all the facilities and established a military government. About 1,200 Australian and European civilians were interned, and most were later deported to Japan or other occupied areas. The Japanese stationed about 3,000 troops on the island and built airfields, gun emplacements, and fortifications, turning Nauru into an important military base. For the Nauruans, the Japanese occupation was catastrophic. The Japanese were harsher than the Australian colonizers, forcing Nauruans into forced labor and imposing strict military control. Food was short and traditional ways of life were completely disrupted. Phosphate mining stopped and the island's economy collapsed. The Japanese occupation began the darkest chapter in Nauru's history, a three-year ordeal of suffering.

events.title: US Air Raids on Nauru
events.description: US Army Air Forces B-24 bombers began intensive bombing of Japanese-occupied Nauru, aiming to destroy the airfields, harbor, and military facilities and to prevent the Japanese from using Nauru as a forward base. The bombing lasted nearly two years, and the island suffered severe destruction. Although the Americans mainly targeted military objectives, the island was small and bombs often hit civilian areas. Many Nauruans were killed or wounded in the raids, and survivors were forced to take shelter in air-raid shelters dug by the Japanese. Houses, churches, and schools were destroyed and infrastructure was badly damaged. The Japanese forced Nauruans to repair facilities and work under dangerous conditions. The air raids intensified hunger and panic on the island. Caught between the warring sides, the Nauruans bore the full suffering of the war. The American bombing weakened the Japanese but also exacted a heavy price from Nauruan civilians. The island was left in ruins, and reconstruction would take years.

events.title: Forced Deportation of Nauruans to Chuuk
events.description: Because of the continued American bombing and serious food shortages, the Japanese military authorities decided to forcibly deport most Nauruans to Chuuk Atoll (then called Truk) in the Caroline Islands. About 1,200 Nauruans were forced onto crowded ships and sailed for several days in terrible conditions. Many died on the voyage of disease and malnutrition. On arrival in Chuuk, the Nauruans were held in harsh camps with scarce food and no medical care, and were forced to do heavy labor. The forced deportation was one of the most tragic events in Nauru's history. Far from home, enduring hunger, disease, and abuse in a foreign land, about 200 Nauruans died during their exile. The survivors saw compatriots and relatives die and suffered deep trauma. The years of suffering on Chuuk left a permanent scar in Nauru's collective memory. The deportation is regarded as a national tragedy of Nauru and is commemorated every year.

events.title: End of the War and Return of the Nauruans
events.description: After Japan's surrender, Australian forces reoccupied Nauru. The Japanese garrison disarmed and surrendered, and the war finally ended. The Nauruans who had survived on Chuuk were found by the Allies in an extremely weak and malnourished state. In early 1946 about 1,000 survivors (about 200 had died) returned home by ship. The Nauruans returned to an island in ruins: buildings were destroyed, phosphate facilities damaged, and the land was covered with bomb craters and mines. Many families had lost loved ones, and the community was deeply traumatized. Yet the return home also brought joy and hope of renewal. The survivors began rebuilding their lives with mixed feelings. The Australian government resumed the trusteeship and promised to help with reconstruction, but aid was slow. In the early postwar period, the Nauruans survived on army rations and relief supplies. Reconstruction was a long process, but the very fact of the nation's survival was a great victory. The experience of the war strengthened Nauruan national identity and the desire for independence.

events.title: United Nations Trust Territory
events.description: After the dissolution of the League of Nations, Nauru became a trust territory under the United Nations system, still jointly administered by Australia, Britain, and New Zealand, with Australia continuing as the administering authority. Compared with the League mandate, the UN trusteeship system in theory demanded greater responsibility, including regular reports to the UN Trusteeship Council, periodic visiting missions, and the ultimate goal of self-government or independence. This provided an international legal framework for the Nauruan independence movement. Australia invested funds to rebuild the war-damaged phosphate facilities and infrastructure, aiming to resume exports as quickly as possible. The British Phosphate Commissioners resumed operations, with extraction exceeding prewar levels. With the postwar global agricultural expansion, demand for fertilizer surged and Nauru's phosphate became even more profitable. Australia nevertheless continued to pay extremely low royalties to Nauruan landowners. The Nauruans began to question this unfair arrangement and demanded a larger share and political rights. The new postwar order laid the foundation for Nauru's struggle for self-determination.

events.title: Rise of Hammer DeRoburt
events.description: Young Nauruan leader Hammer DeRoburt was elected Head Chief of Nauru Local Government Council, beginning decades-long career dominating Nauruan politics. DeRoburt born 1922, Western-educated, fluent in English, familiar with colonial system, while deeply rooted in Nauruan culture and tradition. He represented new generation of Nauruan elite, understanding modern politics while committed to protecting national interests. DeRoburt became main spokesman for Nauruans negotiating with Australian authorities, pursuing more rights and better treatment with firm but diplomatic approach. He led movements for higher royalties, improved social services and expanded political autonomy. DeRoburt possessed charisma and political skills, gaining wide support. His rise marked Nauruan political awakening and beginning of independence movement. DeRoburt became father of Nauruan independence, shaping modern Nauru's political landscape.

events.title: Royalty Negotiations and Struggle
events.description: Led by Hammer DeRoburt, Nauruan leaders began fiercely fighting for substantial increase in phosphate royalties. Few pennies per ton paid by British Phosphate Commissioners was far below market value, Nauruans considered this naked exploitation. Nauruan representatives made reasonable demands, but Australian government long refused substantial increases. Negotiations continued for years, full of frustration. Nauruans petitioned UN Trusteeship Council, international pressure gradually increased. Australian media and public began paying attention to Nauru's plight, some humanitarians and church groups supported Nauruan appeals. By late 1950s, facing sustained pressure, Australian government finally agreed to gradually raise royalties. Though still not completely fair, this was important victory, bringing more income to Nauru. This struggle cultivated Nauruan political consciousness and collective action capacity, laying foundation for later pursuit of complete control over phosphate resources and political independence.

events.title: Curtis Island Relocation Proposal
events.description: Facing projected phosphate depletion within coming decades, Australian government proposed controversial plan: relocate entire Nauruan population to Curtis Island off Queensland coast. Australia argued this would provide Nauruans with larger land and better prospects. However, Nauruan leaders strongly opposed, viewing it as colonialist attempt to eliminate Nauruan nation and state. DeRoburt led resistance movement, insisting Nauruans had right to remain on ancestral land. This proposal sparked strong nationalist sentiment, uniting Nauruan society. Nauruans petitioned UN, international opinion mostly supported Nauru. Facing determined opposition and international criticism, Australia finally withdrew proposal in 1967. This struggle became important moment in Nauru's pursuit of self-determination, strengthening independence movement's legitimacy. It proved Nauruans unwilling to surrender national sovereignty, even facing environmental challenges.

events.title: Legislative and Executive Councils Established
events.description: Australia agreed to expand Nauruan autonomy, establishing Legislative and Executive Councils, granting Nauruans more self-governing powers. Legislative Council composed of 18 elected members could make laws and budgets, but still required Australian Administrator approval. Executive Council composed of members elected by parliament, responsible for managing internal affairs. Hammer DeRoburt elected Chairman of Executive Council, effectively becoming leader of Nauru's self-governing government. This system was transitional stage toward full independence, letting Nauruans gain actual management experience. Though foreign affairs and defense still controlled by Australia, Nauru now possessed substantial autonomy in internal affairs. New institutions immediately began preparing for full independence, drafting post-independence constitutional framework and policy framework. This was crucial step in Nauru's journey toward sovereign statehood.

events.title: Constitution Drafting and Independence Preparation
events.description: Nauru Legislative Council cooperated with Australian government, beginning to draft independence constitution. Constitution drafting process involved extensive community consultation, balancing modern democratic institutions with traditional customs. Constitution established Nauru as presidential republic, with president elected by parliament for three-year term. Parliament single-chamber, 18 members elected by universal suffrage. Constitution guaranteed basic human rights, freedom of speech and rule of law. Special clauses protected Nauruan ownership of phosphate resources, crucial economic asset. Constitution also preserved traditional land ownership, respecting matrilineal inheritance system. Simultaneously, Nauru trained civil servants, established government departments, preparing to assume all administrative functions. Australia provided technical assistance and financial support, facilitating transition. Independence date set for January 31, 1968. Entire process demonstrated Nauru's determination and capacity for complete autonomy.

events.title: Independence of Nauru
events.description: Nauru formally declared independence, becoming the world's smallest republic and the third smallest country (after the Vatican and Monaco). Independence celebrations were held across the island, and Hammer DeRoburt was elected the first president. Officials from Australia, New Zealand, and Britain attended the ceremony to formally hand over sovereignty. The Nauruan flag was raised for the first time: the blue background symbolizes the Pacific Ocean and the sky, the yellow stripe represents the equator (Nauru lies 26 miles south of it), and the twelve-pointed star symbolizes the twelve traditional tribes. The national anthem "Nauru Bwiema" (Nauru, Our Homeland) was sung. Independence marked the end of colonial rule and the realization of national self-determination. However, Nauru faced enormous challenges: tiny territory (21 square kilometers), a population of only about 6,000, an economy entirely dependent on phosphate, and severe environmental damage. But with hope and pride, the Nauruans began a new chapter as an independent nation. It was an important moment in the wave of decolonization in the Pacific island states.

events.title: Joining the United Nations
events.description: Less than a year after independence, Nauru applied to join the United Nations, but its tiny size provoked controversy. Some countries questioned whether Nauru could bear the obligations and dues of UN membership. However, Nauru insisted on the principle of the equality of sovereign states and held that small states have the same right to take part in the international community. After debate, the UN took Nauru's special circumstances into account and allowed it to join at a lower rate of contributions. Nauru was admitted as the 189th member of the UN, a formal recognition by the international community of its sovereignty. Nauru then joined the Commonwealth, the Pacific Community, and other international organizations. As one of the smallest UN members, Nauru actively participated in the Alliance of Small Island States (AOSIS), advocating for the rights of small island states, environmental protection, and climate justice. UN membership gave Nauru an international platform, and its voice, though small, has legitimate standing in global affairs.

events.title: First Parliamentary Elections
events.description: Nauru held first formal parliamentary elections after independence, electing 18 members to parliament. Elections conducted in fair and transparent atmosphere, voter turnout extremely high, almost all eligible voters participated. Though Nauru had no formal party system (remains so today), candidates ran as individuals based on family ties, tribal loyalty and personal prestige. Election results reflected factional nature of Nauruan politics, with MPs forming informal alliances. Hammer DeRoburt with prestige as independence father and political skills was reelected president, gaining parliamentary majority support. Elections established foundation for Nauruan democratic institutions, but also exposed small state political challenges: kinship and personal alliances dominated politics, policy debates sometimes overshadowed by interpersonal relationships, political stability fragile. Nevertheless, Nauru maintained tradition of regular elections, commendable among Pacific island nations.

events.title: Establishing Diplomatic Relations Network
events.description: Post-independence Nauru began building international diplomatic relations network. Beyond close ties with former trustee powers Australia, Britain and New Zealand, Nauru established diplomatic links with Pacific neighbors including Fiji, Papua New Guinea and other island nations. Nauru also established relations with some Asian countries like Japan, Philippines and Taiwan, these countries having commercial interest in Nauruan phosphate. With limited resources, Nauru couldn't establish many embassies abroad, mainly relying on non-resident ambassadors and consulates. Nauru's representative offices in Australia and New Zealand became main bases for diplomatic activities. Small state diplomacy challenge lies in building effective international presence with limited resources. Nauru adopted pragmatic approach, prioritizing development of relations with countries providing aid and trade opportunities. Diplomatic recognition itself became asset, Nauru learned to use its UN vote and diplomatic recognition as leverage in negotiating with larger countries.

events.title: Acquisition of the Phosphate Industry
events.description: The Nauruan government bought the entire phosphate mining and export operation from the British Phosphate Commissioners, paying 21 million Australian dollars in compensation. It was the most important act of economic sovereignty since independence, achieving full control over the nation's main resource. The government established the Nauru Phosphate Corporation (NPC), a state monopoly directly managing extraction, processing, and sales. All profits belonged to the Nauruan government and landowners. Phosphate revenue then surged, and the oil crisis of the 1970s pushed up fertilizer prices, bringing Nauru an unprecedented boom. Phosphate revenue funded free education, healthcare, housing, and public services. Nauruans enjoyed a high standard of living and paid almost no taxes. The government began investing overseas, buying real estate and businesses in an effort to build a long-term source of income for after the phosphate ran out. This period is seen as Nauru's golden age, but it also sowed the seeds of future problems.

events.title: Joining the Commonwealth
events.description: Nauru became Commonwealth special member, unique arrangement reflecting its tiny size and limited resources. As special member, Nauru participated in some Commonwealth activities but didn't attend Commonwealth Heads of Government Meetings (CHOGM), reducing financial burden. This status allowed Nauru access to Commonwealth technical assistance, education programs and development funds, while maintaining links with former trustee powers Australia and Britain. Though Nauru was never British colony (but German colony), it had connections to British imperial system through Australian trusteeship, adopting Westminster parliamentary system. Commonwealth membership provided Nauru with diplomatic platform and international network, helping newly independent small nation establish international presence. In 2000, Nauru upgraded to full Commonwealth membership, with rights and obligations same as other members. Commonwealth connection is important component of Nauru's international relations.

events.title: Air Nauru Established
events.description: Nauruan government using phosphate wealth established Air Nauru, symbol of Nauru's independence and prosperity. Airline purchased Boeing 727 and 737 jets, operating regular international routes connecting Australia, New Zealand, Fiji, Guam, Philippines and other Pacific destinations. Air Nauru broke island's isolation, facilitating Nauruan travel, trade and international connections. Aircraft painted in Nauruan flag colors, becoming symbol of national pride. Government also used airline for charter services and overseas investment transportation. However, airline never truly profitable, high operating costs and limited passenger base made it dependent on government subsidies. During 1990s economic crisis, Air Nauru fell into serious financial difficulties, aircraft seized for debt, services disrupted. In 2005 airline finally went bankrupt, symbolizing end of prosperity era. 2006 restarted with smaller aircraft, but scale much reduced. Air Nauru's rise and fall reflected nation's economic ups and downs.

events.title: Land Rights and Royalty Disputes
events.description: Nauruan society internally erupted disputes over phosphate royalty distribution. Though government received huge revenues from phosphate exports, landowners felt their compensation remained insufficient. Nauruan traditional land ownership complex, land passing through matrilineal inheritance, rights dispersed among multiple family members. Phosphate mining destroyed land, making it permanently unsuitable for cultivation or habitation, landowners believed they should receive higher compensation. Government and landowner representatives engaged in difficult negotiations, finally agreeing to raise royalty payment standards, establishing more transparent distribution mechanism. However, disputes continued, some families questioned distribution fairness, internal contradictions occasionally erupted. This issue highlighted resource wealth distribution complexity, and tension between traditional land ownership and modern mining industry. Relations between landowners and government, among landowners became ongoing issue in Nauruan politics, affecting social cohesion.

events.title: Economic Prosperity Peak
events.description: Mid-1970s, Nauru reached economic prosperity peak, per capita GDP once among world's highest. Phosphate exports brought this nation of only 6,000 people tens of millions of dollars annually. Government provided generous welfare to all citizens: free education and healthcare, subsidized housing and food, even free overseas education scholarships. Many Nauruan families owned multiple cars (on island only 21 square kilometers!), modern appliances and imported luxury goods. Air Nauru operated regular international flights, Nauru Shipping Line owned fleet. Government invested in real estate in Australia, Hawaii, Philippines and USA, purchasing office buildings, hotels and properties worth hundreds of millions. These investments aimed to create permanent income streams. However, prosperity also brought problems: dependence on imported food led to health issues, lack of work culture, investment mismanagement. For many Nauruans, these were good times, but unsustainable.

events.title: Nauru Becomes Tax Haven
events.description: Nauru began developing offshore finance industry as revenue source beyond phosphate. Government enacted lenient company registration laws, allowing foreigners to register companies at low cost with almost no regulatory requirements. Nauru became tax haven and offshore financial center, thousands of shell companies registered. Banking secrecy laws attracted legitimate businessmen but also used for money laundering and tax evasion. Russian mafia and other criminal organizations reportedly used Nauruan banks to transfer illicit funds. Nauru earned millions from registration fees and banking operations. However, this damaged Nauru's international reputation. In early 2000s, OECD and Financial Action Task Force (FATF) blacklisted Nauru for money laundering and non-cooperative tax jurisdiction. International pressure eventually forced Nauru to clean up offshore finance industry in 2000s, but this period left stain.

events.title: Education Development and Overseas Scholarships
events.description: Nauruan government using phosphate wealth heavily invested in education, establishing free public education system covering primary through high school. Government also provided generous overseas scholarship programs, funding Nauruan students to pursue higher education in Australia, New Zealand and other countries, completely free including tuition, living expenses and travel. Hundreds of Nauruan students benefited, studying various fields including medicine, engineering, law, education and business. Government hoped to cultivate highly educated talent, preparing for national modernization and future development. Many overseas graduates returned to Nauru, working in government, education and business sectors, becoming modernized elite class. However, many chose to remain abroad, causing brain drain. Education investment was one of most positive legacies of Nauru's prosperity era, cultivating generation of well-educated citizens. But after economic crisis, government couldn't maintain same level of education investment, quality declined.

events.title: Emerging Health Crisis
events.description: With lifestyle changes brought by phosphate wealth, Nauru began facing serious public health crisis. Traditional fishing and agricultural lifestyle abandoned, Nauruans completely dependent on imported foods, especially high-sugar, high-fat processed foods. Physical activity decreased, many people no longer needed to work. This led to obesity rates sharply rising, Nauru becoming one of countries with world's highest obesity rates. Accompanying was Type 2 diabetes outbreak, prevalence reaching alarming 30-40%, world's highest. Kidney disease, cardiovascular disease and hypertension also prevalent. Nauru's medical system unable to cope with chronic disease crisis. Many serious cases needed to be sent to Australia for treatment, costs high. Health crisis lowered life expectancy, affected labor productivity, caused huge social and economic burden. This was tragic case of 'diseases of affluence' in poor small nation, consequences continuing today.

events.title: Nauruan Cultural Revival Movement
events.description: Facing modernization and Westernization impact, some Nauruans began worrying about traditional culture loss. Younger generation increasingly alienated from traditional language, customs and knowledge. Responding to this trend, community leaders and cultural workers initiated cultural revival movement, efforts to protect and revive Nauruan cultural heritage. Government supported these efforts, adding Nauruan language and culture teaching to school curriculum, recording oral histories and traditional knowledge, supporting traditional arts and crafts. Though Nauruan language remained main language, English use increasingly common, especially in education and government. Traditional songs, dances and ceremonies were recorded and performed, showcased at national celebrations like Independence Day. However, modern lifestyle and globalization pressures persisted, many traditional practices already lost or preserved only as cultural displays. Cultural revival ongoing struggle, reflecting small nations' challenge maintaining cultural identity in modern world.

events.title: DeRoburt's Political Dominance
events.description: Hammer DeRoburt continued dominating Nauruan politics; since 1968 independence, except brief periods, he remained president. DeRoburt established personal authority and extensive political network, maintaining power through patronage relationships and political skills. His long rule brought relative stability to Nauru but also raised criticism of excessive power concentration. Opposition accused DeRoburt of authoritarian tendencies, lack of transparency and accountability. Phosphate revenue distribution, overseas investment decisions and government contracts became contentious issues. DeRoburt's supporters argued he was effective leader who guided Nauru through early independence and achieved prosperity. Critics believed lack of effective oversight led to resource waste and corruption. This political pattern reflected small state leader's dilemma: balance between strong leadership and democratic checks. DeRoburt ruled until 1989, after which politics became more unstable.

events.title: Phosphate Production Begins Declining
events.description: By mid-1980s, Nauruan phosphate production began obviously declining. After nearly 80 years intensive mining, highest quality and most easily mined deposits were depleted. Remaining reserves were lower quality, requiring higher costs but selling at lower prices. Output fell from 1970s peak of 2 million tons annually to below 1.5 million tons, continuing downward trend. Export revenues decreased, but government and people struggled to accept prosperity ending, continuing to maintain high spending levels. During this period, some visionary leaders warned of need for economic diversification and fiscal discipline, but reform faced resistance. Vested interests, political pressure and lack of alternative industries made transition difficult. Nauru failed to effectively prepare for post-phosphate era, missing opportunity to use wealth to build sustainable economic foundation. Production decline was harbinger of coming economic crisis.

events.title: DeRoburt's Fall from Power
events.description: After 21 years of intermittent rule (1968-1976, 1978-1989), Hammer DeRoburt fell in parliamentary no-confidence vote, Kennan Adeang elected president. DeRoburt's fall partly stemmed from dissatisfaction with his long dominance, partly from concerns about economic prospects and criticism of phosphate management. Nauruan politics entered more unstable period, frequent presidential changes became norm. DeRoburt was reelected in 1992 but fell again in 1995, dying same year from health problems. His death marked end of an era. DeRoburt was hailed as father of Nauruan independence and founder of modern Nauru, but his legacy complex: successful in achieving independence and sovereignty, but failed to ensure nation's long-term economic sustainability. His era witnessed Nauru's transformation from colony to wealthy nation, but also planted seeds of eventual crisis.

events.title: Environmental Rehabilitation Discussion Begins
events.description: Facing massive environmental destruction, Nauruan government and international community began discussing possibility of land rehabilitation. About 80% of island's central area already destroyed by mining, leaving moonscape. Scientific assessments showed rehabilitation extremely difficult and expensive: need to remove limestone pinnacles, fill deep pits, import massive amounts of topsoil, replant vegetation. Costs estimated at hundreds of millions to billions of dollars, far beyond Nauru's capacity. Australia, UN and environmental organizations provided technical assistance, conducted small-scale pilot projects, but progress slow. Main obstacles included lack of funding, technical challenges and insufficient political will. Some Nauruans questioned whether worth investing in rehabilitating already destroyed land, rather than focusing on protecting remaining habitable areas. Environmental rehabilitation became Nauru's long-term agenda, but still no substantial progress today, damaged land basically remains barren. This is cautionary case of irreversible environmental destruction.

events.title: International Court of Justice Settlement Agreement
events.description: Nauru reached out-of-court settlement with Australia, Britain and New Zealand on environmental compensation lawsuit. Three countries agreed to jointly pay 107 million Australian dollars to Nauru for environmental rehabilitation. Australia paid majority (about 107 million), Britain and New Zealand paid symbolic amounts. Settlement avoided lengthy legal battle and uncertain outcome. However, amount far below Nauru's initial demands, also far insufficient to completely rehabilitate damaged land. Settlement funds established special trust fund, theoretically for rehabilitation projects. But in reality, fund management poor, some diverted to other uses. Actual rehabilitation work progressed limited. Nevertheless, settlement had important significance in international law, establishing former colonial countries' legal and moral responsibility for colonial-era environmental destruction. This provided precedent for other former colonies pursuing compensation. For Nauru, this was belated justice, but couldn't compensate for damage already done.

events.title: First Female MP
events.description: Nauru elected first female Member of Parliament, marking progress in gender equality, though progress slow. Nauru is traditional patriarchal society, politics long dominated by men. Women play important roles in family and community, but public political participation limited. Matrilineal land inheritance system gave women certain economic power, but political power remained in male hands. First female MP's election was breakthrough, showing societal attitudes beginning to change. However, women's political participation remained very limited, female representation in parliament extremely low. Gender inequality, domestic violence and women's education opportunities gradually gaining attention. Nauru signed Convention on Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women (CEDAW), committing to improve gender equality. But actual progress slow, cultural traditions and social norms deeply entrenched. Women's empowerment is important but unfinished agenda in Nauru's modernization process.

events.title: DeRoburt's Death
events.description: Nauru's independence father Hammer DeRoburt died aged 73, marking end of an era. DeRoburt led Nauruan independence movement since 1950s, served as president 1968-1995 except brief periods, was modern Nauru's most influential political figure. His death triggered national mourning, state funeral held, Pacific regional leaders attended tribute. DeRoburt's legacy complex and contradictory: he successfully led Nauru to independence and sovereignty, created unprecedented prosperity in 1970s; but also failed to ensure economic sustainability, over-reliant on phosphate, investment mismanagement. His long rule both provided stability and limited political pluralism. Historians diverge on assessment: some view him as national hero and visionary leader, others criticize paternalistic rule and policy mistakes. Regardless of assessment, DeRoburt undoubtedly shaped independent Nauru's first 25 years, his influence remains profound today.

events.title: Currency Reform
events.description: Nauru always used Australian dollar as official currency, but government began issuing own commemorative coins, mainly for collection rather than circulation. These coins featured Nauruan history, culture and nature, aiming to increase national revenue and raise international profile. However, this scheme had limited commercial success. Nauru continued using Australian dollar as main currency, because its economic scale too small to maintain independent monetary policy, and closely linked to Australian economy. Using Australian dollar provided monetary stability, facilitated trade and financial transactions with Australia, but also meant Nauru lacked monetary policy tools to address economic crisis. Nauru completely dependent on Reserve Bank of Australia's policy. This is another manifestation of small state's limited economic sovereignty: must choose between monetary independence and stability, most choose stability.

events.title: Modernization of Communications Infrastructure
events.description: Nauru began to modernize its communications infrastructure, introducing digital telephone exchanges, internet connectivity, and mobile phone service. Before this, Nauru's communications technology was backward, and international calls were expensive and unreliable. The modernization was supported by aid funds and private investment. The arrival of the internet opened a new window for Nauru, allowing islanders to access global information and contact relatives and friends overseas. Email and later social media changed the way people communicated. The government also began exploring e-government and digital services. However, the internet infrastructure was limited, with low bandwidth, high costs, and low penetration. Nauru depended on submarine cables and satellite links to the outside world, which were fragile and expensive. The digital divide was real: the wealthy and educated could make full use of technology, while the poor were excluded. Communications modernization was progress but also highlighted the infrastructure challenges of small island states and their dependence on external technology.

events.title: Millennium Celebrations and Outlook
events.description: Nauru celebrated the arrival of the new millennium together with the world, but with mixed feelings. Thirty-two years after independence, Nauru stood at a crossroads. The prosperity of the past was now a memory, the phosphate resource was exhausted, the economy was in difficulty, overseas investments had failed, and government finances were strained. But the Nauruans remained hopeful, believing they could overcome the challenges and find a new path of development. The millennium celebration was held in front of Parliament House, where the president gave a speech reviewing past achievements, acknowledging current difficulties, and expressing optimism for the future. Churches held special services, praying for peace and prosperity. The younger generation had expectations of the 21st century, hoping that new technology, globalization, and international cooperation would bring new opportunities for small island states. The millennium also prompted reflection: what lessons had Nauru learned from the phosphate boom? How could it avoid repeating its mistakes? How could it achieve development while protecting its environment and culture? These questions remain relevant, and Nauru continues to look for answers.

events.title: Environmental Destruction Becomes Apparent
events.description: By 1980, phosphate mining had continued for nearly 80 years and had done catastrophic damage to Nauru's environment. About 80 percent of the land in the central highland of the island had been mined out, leaving jagged limestone pinnacles and deep pits, a moonscape unfit for habitation or cultivation. The topsoil was completely removed, vegetation disappeared, and the ecosystem collapsed. Nauru had changed from a lush tropical island into an industrial wasteland. Phosphate dust polluted the air and water and affected residents' health. Residential areas were squeezed into a narrow coastal strip, with severe overcrowding. Traditional agriculture and the subsistence way of life no longer existed, and Nauruans depended entirely on imported food. The severe environmental degradation drew international attention, and environmental organizations criticized it as a textbook case of an "environmental disaster." The Nauruans began to realize the real cost of wealth, but the damage was done, and restoring the land would take billions of dollars and several generations. Environmental destruction became Nauru's greatest long-term challenge.

events.title: Environmental Compensation Case Against Australia
events.description: The Nauruan government sued Australia in the International Court of Justice (ICJ), seeking compensation for the environmental damage done during the trusteeship period (1920–1968). The suit claimed that Australia, as the administering power, had an obligation to protect Nauru's environment and to be responsible for the islanders' welfare, but in practice had plundered resources, destroyed the land, and taken no rehabilitation measures. Nauru demanded hundreds of millions of dollars in compensation to restore the damaged land. Australia at first argued that the court had no jurisdiction, but the court ruled that the case could proceed. It was an important case in international law, involving the retroactive responsibility of former colonial powers for colonial damage. After years of legal struggle, in 1993 the parties reached an out-of-court settlement: Australia, Britain, and New Zealand jointly paid 107 million Australian dollars to Nauru for land rehabilitation. Although the sum was far from enough to restore the environment fully, it was an important moral and legal victory that established the principle of colonial responsibility. The settlement money was used to create a dedicated fund for rehabilitation projects.

events.title: Phosphate Reserves Depletion Crisis
events.description: By the early 1990s, the high-quality phosphate deposits were essentially exhausted. Mining shifted to lower-quality secondary deposits, which cost more to extract and sold for less. Phosphate output and export revenue fell sharply. The Nauru Phosphate Corporation faced financial difficulties and heavy debts. Government revenue dropped abruptly, but generous welfare and public spending were maintained, causing the budget deficit to increase sharply. Nauru began to rely on income from overseas investments, but many of the investments were poorly managed or failed. The government was forced to borrow to keep operating. An economic crisis began to emerge, but the government and public found it hard to accept that the age of prosperity was over and continued to overspend. The exhaustion of phosphate had been foreseen for decades, but Nauru failed to diversify its economy or build a sustainable alternative source of income. The "resource curse" was fully realized in Nauru: abundant resources brought short-term prosperity but led to a distorted economic structure, environmental destruction, and long-term decline.

events.title: Overseas Investment Losses
events.description: Nauru Phosphate Corporation and government's overseas investments in 1970s-80s began massive losses. Many investment decisions lacked professional assessment, full of corruption and cronyism. For example, Nauru House office building purchased in Melbourne Australia plummeted in value, management chaotic. Investments in London real estate, Washington DC properties, Philippine hotels all failed or produced meager returns. Some investments were frauds, advisors absconded with funds. Nauru embroiled in various lawsuits, legal costs high. Estimated hundreds of millions of dollars lost or unrecoverable. These assets supposed to provide income for post-phosphate era became burdens. Government forced to sell assets to pay debts, but often at fire-sale prices. Investment failures stemmed from lack of financial management expertise, political interference, corruption and overconfidence. For small nations, this was painful lesson: sudden wealth requires prudent management, but Nauru lacked institutions and experience. Losses accelerated economic crisis.

events.title: Joining Alliance of Small Island States
events.description: Nauru actively participates in Alliance of Small Island States (AOSIS), becoming one of organization's most determined advocates on climate change issues. As low-elevation coral island, Nauru extremely vulnerable to sea level rise threats. Island's highest point only 71 meters, most population lives in coastal areas, sea level rise of few meters could flood residential zones. Nauru vociferously advocates in international climate negotiations, demanding developed countries reduce greenhouse gas emissions, provide climate adaptation funding. Nauruan representatives deliver moving speeches at UN climate conferences, warning small island nations face existential threats. As one of most vulnerable countries, Nauru's voice carries moral authority. However, as tiny nation, Nauru's actual influence limited. Nauru also seeks climate adaptation funds, building seawalls and infrastructure protection. Climate change became core issue in Nauruan foreign policy, symbolizing small island nations' vulnerability in globalized world.

events.title: Government Fiscal Collapse
events.description: By late 1990s, Nauruan government finances neared collapse. Phosphate revenues almost ceased, overseas investments lost, government had no other significant revenue sources yet maintained huge expenditures. Civil servant salaries delayed for months, triggering strikes. Government services cut, infrastructure deteriorating. Nauru Electricity Corporation couldn't afford fuel, island frequently experienced power outages, sometimes lasting weeks. Water supply unstable, hospitals lacked medicines and equipment. Air Nauru went bankrupt, aircraft seized for debt, international flights stopped, island isolated from world. Government defaulted on employee pensions, store shelves empty, economy nearly ground to halt. Nauru sought help from Taiwan, India and other countries, obtaining emergency loans and aid to maintain basic operations. This was stunning fall from extreme wealth to poverty, taking only over decade. Fiscal crisis exposed fundamental flaws in Nauru's development model: over-reliance on single resource, lack of economic diversification, fiscal mismanagement, corruption and governance failure. Nauru became 'failed state' case study.

events.title: Pacific Solution Agreement
events.description: Facing a fiscal crisis, Nauru reached the controversial "Pacific Solution" agreement with Australia. Under the agreement, Nauru agreed to set up a refugee processing center on the island to receive asylum seekers who tried to enter Australia illegally by boat. Australia intercepted boats at sea and sent the refugees to Nauru (and Manus Island) to have their asylum claims processed. In return, Australia provided the Nauruan government with tens of millions of Australian dollars in aid for budget support, infrastructure, and services. The money was a lifeline for near-bankrupt Nauru. The first refugees arrived in 2001, most of them from Afghanistan, Iraq, and the Middle East. The center was run and funded by Australia and held hundreds of refugees, with processing that could last for years. Human rights organizations harshly criticized the program, saying it held refugees on a remote island in terrible conditions and caused psychological trauma. Nauru was accused of selling out human rights for money. But the Nauruan government argued that it was a sovereign decision and that the aid was used to improve the lives of its own citizens. The agreement defined Nauru's diplomatic and economic situation in the early 21st century.

events.title: Money Laundering Blacklist and Banking Reform
events.description: Under international pressure, especially from OECD and FATF threatening sanctions, Nauru forced to thoroughly reform offshore banking industry. In 1990s, Nauru registered about 400 offshore banks, many suspected of money laundering. US Treasury accused Nauruan banks of being used by Russian criminal organizations to launder billions of dollars. FATF blacklisted Nauru as non-cooperative country, threatening international financial isolation. US considered imposing sanctions on Nauru, possibly cutting off dollar transaction channels, which would be fatal blow to import-dependent Nauru. Nauruan government yielded to pressure, closing all offshore banks, revoking banking licenses, strengthening financial regulation, passing anti-money laundering laws. Australia assisted establishing new regulatory framework. In 2005, FATF removed Nauru from blacklist. Though this restored international credibility, it also cut off important revenue source. Reform period exposed that for survival Nauru had to sacrifice economic sovereignty, accepting external intervention.

events.title: National State of Emergency
events.description: Nauruan government declared national fiscal state of emergency. Treasury nearly empty, unable to pay for basic services. Government defaulted on civil servant salaries for months, triggering strikes. Hospital medicines depleted, schools lacked teaching materials, police had no gasoline for patrols. Electricity company couldn't afford diesel, daily power supply only few hours. Desalination plant shut down, freshwater severely scarce. Communications facilities outdated, phones and internet frequently interrupted. Only flight to outside world also stopped due to Air Nauru bankruptcy, island almost isolated from world. Supermarket shelves empty, residents relied on relatives overseas sending supplies. Diabetes and kidney disease chronic patients lacked treatment, health crisis deepened. International aid agencies provided emergency humanitarian assistance. Australia and Taiwan provided budget support and material aid. This was one of darkest moments in Nauruan history, many citizens considered emigrating. Emergency forced government to undertake radical reforms, restructuring economy and administration.

events.title: Political Instability and Presidential Changes
events.description: Economic crisis triggered serious political instability. Nauru's parliament only 18 seats, weak party system, unstable political alignments, frequent no-confidence motions. During 2003-2004, Nauru changed five presidents in 18 months, governments repeatedly collapsed and reformed. Political factions fiercely opposed around resource allocation, diplomatic relations (especially Taiwan vs China) and power struggles. Some politicians accused of corruption and cronyism. Parliamentary sessions often chaotic due to MP conflicts. This political turmoil paralyzed government functions, hindered reforms and long-term planning. International community lost confidence in Nauru's governance capacity. In 2004, Ludwig Scotty elected president, managed to maintain relative stability, pushing some reforms. However political instability reflected Nauru's deep problems: factional nature of small state politics, zero-sum competition triggered by resource scarcity, institutional fragility. This period exposed Nauruan democratic system's weaknesses, also tested national resilience.

events.title: Upgrade to Full Commonwealth Membership
events.description: Nauru was upgraded from special member to full member of the Commonwealth, gaining rights and obligations equal to those of the other member states. This meant Nauru could now take part in the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) and all Commonwealth institutions. The upgrade reflected the development of Nauru's national capacity and the rise in its international standing. Commonwealth membership gave Nauru a multilateral diplomatic platform, access to channels of aid and technical assistance, and a network of ties with 54 member states. Nauru used Commonwealth forums to advocate for small island state issues, especially climate change and sustainable development. The Commonwealth Secretariat also helped Nauru with governance reform and capacity building. However, full membership also brought a greater financial burden, including dues and the cost of attending meetings, which was a challenge for financially strained Nauru.

events.title: Collapse of Air Nauru
events.description: Air Nauru, which had operated for 30 years, formally declared bankruptcy, a symbolic end to Nauru's age of prosperity. The airline had accumulated huge debts, its aircraft were seized by creditors, and it could not continue operating. The last aircraft was impounded by an Australian court at Melbourne Airport, leaving the Nauruan president and delegation stranded overseas in an embarrassing scene. The airline's bankruptcy almost cut off Nauru's links with the outside world: islanders could not travel, trade was impeded, and economic isolation deepened. It was a heavy blow to a Nauru already in crisis. The government was forced to rely on charter flights and irregular services from neighboring countries' airlines. In 2006 the government relaunched air service with a smaller aircraft (a Boeing 737), but on a much smaller scale than before and with limited routes. The rise and fall of Air Nauru was a microcosm of the whole country's economic ups and downs: from the extravagance of the phosphate boom to the embarrassment of the bankruptcy crisis.

events.title: Establishing Relations with Taiwan
events.description: Nauru established formal diplomatic relations with Republic of China (Taiwan), becoming one of Taiwan's important allies in Pacific. In exchange, Taiwan provided Nauru with substantial economic aid, including budget support, infrastructure projects, scholarships and technical assistance. This aid was crucial for financially struggling Nauru, potentially meaning difference between government functioning or not. Taiwan funded road construction, wharves, government buildings, upgraded power systems, provided medical equipment. Taiwan also dispatched technical teams to assist agricultural and fisheries development. In return, Nauru supported Taiwan at UN and international venues, fighting for Taiwan's international space. However, this relationship also involved Nauru in cross-strait politics. Mainland China pressured Nauru to break with Taiwan, recognize One China principle, promising larger-scale aid. Nauru's choice between two sides became core foreign policy issue, also triggering internal political divisions. Some criticized Nauru for selling diplomatic recognition for aid, but government argued this was small state reality.

events.title: Fisheries License Agreements
events.description: Facing economic difficulties, Nauru began more actively utilizing fisheries resources in its Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ). Nauru's EEZ covers about 312,000 square kilometers, far larger than land area, rich in tuna and other fish. Nauru signed fisheries license agreements with foreign fishing companies (mainly from Japan, Taiwan, South Korea and China), allowing them to fish in Nauruan waters in exchange for license fees. This became important government revenue source, bringing millions of dollars annually. Nauru also joined Forum Fisheries Agency (FFA) and Western and Central Pacific Fisheries Commission (WCPFC), participating in regional fisheries management. However, Nauru lacked effective monitoring and enforcement capacity, Illegal, Unreported and Unregulated (IUU) fishing serious problem. Overfishing threatened sustainability of fish stocks. Nauru tried to balance maximizing fisheries revenues with protecting marine resources, challenge commonly faced by Pacific island nations.

events.title: Renewable Energy Initiatives
events.description: Nauru began exploring renewable energy sources to reduce dependence on costly imported diesel fuel for power generation. Government cooperated with Australia, Asian Development Bank and international environmental organizations, initiating solar energy projects. Small-scale solar panels installed on government buildings, schools and health centers. However, progress slow due to lack of funding, technical capacity and maintenance challenges. Nauru's tropical marine climate (high humidity, salt corrosion) posed challenges for solar equipment longevity. Island's electricity demand fluctuated, diesel generators still needed as backup. Despite challenges, renewable energy represented important direction for sustainable development. Nauru also explored utilizing ocean currents and wind energy, but projects remained experimental stage. Energy security and cost remained major concerns for import-dependent Nauru. Transition to renewable energy was long-term goal, requiring sustained international support and technical assistance.

events.title: Recognizing Kosovo and Abkhazia
events.description: In controversial diplomatic move, Nauru recognized independence of Kosovo and Abkhazia (breakaway region from Georgia). These recognitions occurred in context of Nauru seeking financial assistance, with Russia reportedly providing economic aid in exchange for Abkhazia recognition. Nauru became one of few countries recognizing Abkhazia, joining Russia, Venezuela, Nicaragua and Syria. This angered Georgia and Western countries, viewing Nauru as selling diplomatic recognition. Nauru also recognized Kosovo's independence from Serbia, putting it on opposing side from Russia on this issue, but aligning with US and most EU countries. These decisions illustrated reality of small state diplomacy: diplomatic recognition as tradeable commodity, exchanged for financial aid. Nauru faced accusations of 'checkbook diplomacy', but government defended sovereign right to conduct independent foreign policy. This episode highlighted Nauru's diplomatic pragmatism and financial desperation, also exposed ethical dilemmas of small states.

events.title: Climate Change Impacts Intensify
events.description: In the 2010s Nauru increasingly felt the effects of climate change. Sea levels gradually rose, and at high tide seawater flooded low-lying coastal areas and eroded the shoreline. Storms increased in intensity and frequency, causing more damage. Rainfall patterns changed, and longer dry spells threatened the limited freshwater supply. Ocean acidification affected coral reefs and marine ecosystems, threatening fishery resources. Extreme heat events became more frequent, affecting health and comfort. As a low-lying coral island, Nauru is extremely vulnerable to climate change. Scientists predict that unless action is taken to limit global warming, parts of Nauru could become uninhabitable within this century. The government invested in adaptation measures, including building sea walls, improving drainage, strengthening building standards, and diversifying water sources. Nauru became one of the most vocal advocates in international climate negotiations, demanding that developed countries make deep emission cuts and provide climate finance. Climate change changed from an abstract threat into a real crisis, affecting Nauruans' daily lives and the nation's future.

events.title: Violence at the Refugee Center
events.description: Serious violence broke out at the Nauru refugee processing center. Long detention, harsh conditions, processing delays, and an uncertain future left the refugees extremely frustrated and desperate. The protests escalated into riots, facilities were set on fire and damaged, and refugees and security personnel were injured. The incident drew international attention and criticism, and human rights organizations, doctors, and UN officials harshly condemned conditions at the center. Reports revealed overcrowding, heat, lack of privacy, inadequate medical care, and a mental health crisis. Child refugees suffered particularly severe trauma. The Australian and Nauruan governments came under pressure to improve conditions or close the center. Australia invested more in improving facilities, but the basic policy did not change. The Nauruan government reacted defensively to international criticism, restricting access by the media and human rights organizations. The refugee issue became the main stain on Nauru's international image, overshadowing the other challenges the island nation faced. Nauru was caught in a moral dilemma: it needed Australia's money, but the price was participating in a controversial human rights policy.

events.title: Judicial Independence Dispute
events.description: Serious conflict broke out between the Nauruan government and the judiciary, triggering a constitutional crisis. The government revoked the residence permits of several foreign judges (mainly from Australia), in effect expelling them. These judges had made rulings unfavorable to the government, including in cases related to refugees and the opposition. The government also abolished the right of appeal to the High Court of Australia, cutting off the last channel of judicial review. Critics accused the government of undermining judicial independence and establishing authoritarian rule. International legal organizations, the Australian Bar Association, and human rights organizations harshly condemned these actions. Opposition members of parliament and activists faced political persecution, and some were prosecuted and imprisoned on charges that included protesting and disrupting parliamentary order. Media freedom and the space for civil society were severely squeezed. The Nauruan government argued that it was defending sovereignty and resisting foreign interference. However, these actions marked a serious backsliding of Nauru's democratic institutions and raised widespread concern about the rule of law and human rights.

events.title: Pacific Islands Forum Issues
events.description: Nauru actively participated in the Pacific Islands Forum (PIF), promoting a common agenda of small island states. The Forum is the most important regional organization of the Pacific island countries, discussing economic development, climate change, fisheries management, regional security, and diplomatic coordination. Nauru was especially concerned with climate change, the protection of ocean resources, and the effects of great-power competition on the Pacific. Forum members debated China's growing influence in the Pacific; some countries (such as Australia and the Federated States of Micronesia) expressed concern, while others (including Nauru) defended sovereign choice. The Forum also discussed the Taiwan issue; Nauru, as a diplomatic ally of Taiwan, supported Taiwan's participation in regional affairs in some form. The PIF gave Nauru a platform for equal dialogue with larger neighbors, where a collective voice has more influence than acting alone. Regional cooperation is vital for small island states in addressing common challenges, and Nauru actively used this mechanism.

events.title: Human Rights Record Draws Scrutiny
events.description: Nauru's human rights record drew harsh criticism from the United Nations and international human rights organizations. The main concerns included poor conditions at the refugee processing center, damage to judicial independence, persecution of the opposition, severe restrictions on media freedom, and a squeezed space for civil society. UN special rapporteurs and the human rights committee criticized Nauru many times and called for reform. Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch issued reports documenting violations. Australia was also criticized for cooperating with Nauru on refugee policy. The Nauruan government reacted strongly to the criticism, accusing foreign powers of interfering in its sovereignty, Western bias, and double standards. The government stressed the existential challenges facing Nauru and argued that Western countries did not understand the reality of small island states. However, Nauru's democracy scores and human rights rankings continued to fall, affecting its international reputation and access to aid. Some donor countries considered linking aid to human rights improvements. This put pressure on the Nauruan government, but reform progressed slowly and political will was limited. Human rights became a continuing point of friction in Nauru's relations with the international community.

events.title: Relations with the International Criminal Court
events.description: Nauru is a state party to the International Criminal Court (ICC) and supports international justice and accountability for the most serious crimes. As a small country, Nauru has no resources to prosecute war crimes or crimes against humanity, and the ICC provides the necessary international mechanism. Nauru has spoken actively on ICC matters, especially on climate change and environmental destruction. Some Nauruan advocates have proposed including serious environmental destruction (ecocide) among the crimes under ICC jurisdiction, so that individuals and companies causing large-scale environmental damage could be prosecuted. This relates to Nauru's own experience: the devastating environmental destruction caused by phosphate mining. Although the proposal has not yet succeeded, it reflects the growing importance of climate and environmental justice in international law. Nauru's support for the ICC also reflects its commitment to a rules-based international order, though given its own questioned human rights record this contradiction has drawn some criticism.

events.title: Closure of the Refugee Center
events.description: In 2008 Australia's new government (Kevin Rudd's Labor government) abolished the Pacific Solution policy and closed the refugee processing center on Nauru. The last refugees and staff left, and the facilities stood idle. It was a major blow to Nauru's economy, since the aid and jobs brought by the operation of the center had sustained the island's economy in the 2000s. Hundreds of jobs disappeared, and the government budget again faced a gap. Nauru lost one of its main sources of income. The government was forced to look for new economic opportunities and aid partners. Some Nauruans regretted the closure of the center, despite the moral controversy it had brought. Human rights organizations praised Australia for ending an "inhumane" policy. The closure exposed the fragility of Nauru's economy: overreliance on foreign aid and a single source of income, and a lack of an independent economic base.
